title: Qualcomm to cut jobs worldwide in performance-focused layoffs, internal memo shows
author: B
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Qualcomm plans worldwide job cuts following annual employee reviews, Reuters reported October 20, citing an internal memo from CEO Cristiano Amon. Notifications are scheduled to begin in November, but the number of affected positions remains undisclosed. Amon described the initiative as a “performance-focused reduction,” with business priorities, organizational needs, and employee expertise informing decisions. The report also places the cuts against weaker consumer electronics demand and Qualcomm’s efforts to expand beyond smartphones.

Why does this matter? For a semiconductor designer, workforce decisions influence more than operating expenses. Engineering knowledge accumulates across product generations, customer relationships, software development, and difficult technical investigations. Losing that experience can create costs that emerge well after payroll savings appear.

The management challenge is distinguishing persistent individual underperformance from organizational problems. Missed targets can reflect unclear priorities, inadequate resources, shifting requirements, or dependencies outside an employee’s control. Effective reviews should examine those conditions before treating performance ratings as a complete explanation.

The memo’s emphasis on evolving skills also raises questions about redeployment. When business requirements change, some employees may benefit from training or reassignment. Others may possess valuable expertise that fits a different team. Evaluating those options can help preserve institutional knowledge while supporting new commercial priorities.

Employees will watch how consistently the process operates. Clear criteria, respectful communication, and credible explanations can influence whether remaining teams retain confidence in leadership. Uncertainty can also encourage experienced staff to seek opportunities elsewhere, potentially widening disruption beyond the planned reductions.

For customers and partners, the relevant issue is continuity: whether Qualcomm maintains development schedules, technical support, and dependable execution.

The eventual test is operational. Lower headcount alone does not demonstrate stronger performance. Qualcomm must show that its organization can deliver competitive products, retain essential capabilities, and pursue growth without weakening the engineering foundations on which future revenue depends.
